title: LangSmith Tool Gateway: Secure, governed tool use for agents
summary: LangSmith Tool Gateway, now in Public Beta, handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, with policies, approvals, and traces.
story_key: story|title:langsmith tool gateway secure governed tool use for agents
content_excerpt: Agents are moving beyond the chat window to take on more proactive and ambient work. Instead of waiting for a prompt, they run on a schedule or are triggered by events, and they’re handling longer tasks without someone checking every step. That makes them much more useful, but it also means teams need to control which tools each agent can call and whose identity it acts with, and keep a record of every action it takes. Today, we’re launching LangSmith Tool Gateway in Public Beta, on the LangSmith Agent Platform . Tool Gateway is a managed tool layer that handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, making it simple to govern the actions your agents take. Tool Gateway makes it easier and faster for engineering teams to grant agents access to new tools in a controlled manner and without hand-rolling auth each time. Security and compliance teams can use LangSmith to trace and audit tool calls as part of agent monitoring. When agents are in production, platform teams need visibility into what each agent did, controls over which tools and models it can use, and usage policies that limit spend and risk. With LangSmith, developers can build, run, and improve agents in a single platform. LLM Gateway governs the model calls agents make. With it, you can set spend limits and model fallbacks, add rate limits, redact personal data and secrets, and provides visibility within the agent trace with rich information on model calls such as latency, fallbacks, failures, guardrails triggered, etc. Tool Gateway lives in LangSmith alongside LLM Gateway, and provides governance across this lifecycle. Tool Gateway simplifies tool lists for agents, implementing policies on usage, managing identity for tool use, and as with LLM Gateway, provides visibility within the agent trace through rich information on tool calls such as servers, users, outcomes, latency, etc. Together, Tool Gateway and LLM Gateway provide comprehensive visibility and governance over agent actions and spend. Agents in production need to serve hundreds or thousands of users, each with their own set of permissions. This means managing and refreshing a large volume of tokens, and carefully managing and recording access for security and audit requirements. Managing identity and visibility at scale is orders of magnitude more difficult than local development. title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
summary: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.

title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
summary: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.

title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
summary: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
summary: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.

title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
summary: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

content_excerpt: Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform : a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business. In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next. 2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses , models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work . Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models. Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing , monitoring , and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals. AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened. We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple. title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
summary: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three  million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption.
story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level.   • Changed a managed-mcp.json added mid-session so it may apply at the next check; restart open sessions for it to apply in full
  • Changed Code Mode's $ shell helper to refuse some values with an error; nothing runs
  • Changed auto mode to stop some shell commands that ran before
  • Changed some Bash commands on macOS that ran before to ask or be refused
  • Changed a hook's "decision": "block" to hold in more cases, so a hook that always prints one may start blocking calls
  • Changed sessions that start in auto by default to take a server-managed defaultMode once settings load, or Manual if settings fail with no stored copy and policy fails or requires it
  • Changed auto mode for organizations with the Claude Code + Cowork HIPAA configuration: on a direct Anthropic API connection, the server-side classifier now checks actions, as for other organizations
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to keep its state in some cases during a session, until you run /sandbox or /cd; Bash may ask first
  • Changed sandboxed commands on macOS, Linux and WSL to no longer write to some sensitive home folders by default; some can be allowed with sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite in user or managed settings
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to set aside unexpected entries in a repository's .git folder after a command
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on Linux and WSL to create some missing --add-dir folders before each sandboxed command, so commands that create them can fail, skip, or land inside them
  • Changed commands that a permission hook or SDK host rewrites while approving to stay in the sandbox if the original was checked as sandboxed; the approver can add dangerouslyDisableSandbox: true
  • Changed claude mcp serve to ignore sandbox.excludedCommands
  • Changed /rewind on macOS, Linux and WSL to leave some files untouched and report them as skipped when the sandbox is on
  • Changed the Bash sandbox to ask before some lines that set environment variables when auto-allow is off; unattended runs can refuse them
  • Changed Claude's file tools to refuse writes to Claude Code's sign-in files, such as .credentials.json
  • Changed the Bash permission check to ask before more commands reach Claude Code's sign-in files
  • Changed some file tools to refuse some device and process files
  • Changed some cp and mv commands to ask first
  • Changed some tool calls in bypass permissions mode to ask for approval, or be denied where no one can be asked
  • Changed the Bash permission check to ask about some commands with very long values it can't finish checking, or to refuse them where a deny rule may apply or no one can answer
  • Changed subagents isolated in a worktree to refuse, in any repository, some git commands in Bash that can rewrite branches shared with your checkout; sessions are not affected
  • Changed ExitWorktree to refuse removing a worktree while a background subagent or shell command may still be running in it, unless Claude passes discard_changes
  • Changed the computer use macOS permissions panel to ignore j and k; the arrow keys and Ctrl+P/Ctrl+N still move the selection
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before some more commands; unattended runs refuse them unless an allow rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows them
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask about some more commands, even in bypass permissions mode, and to refuse some of them
  • Changed some malformed PowerShell commands to be denied
  • Changed some PowerShell tool commands that define a function named like a built-in command to be refused, so Claude can rename it
  • Changed auto mode to ignore some wildcard shell allow rules, such as ones that name no program or that start with $HOME, so the safety check decides those commands
  • Changed auto mode to judge wildcard allow rules whose program is a Windows backslash path, so those calls can be blocked; exact rules keep their allow; we plan to restore rules that start with .\
  • Changed a managed autoMode.environment list without "$defaults" to replace every built-in entry in Claude Desktop and Agent SDK apps too; add "$defaults" or copy the sensitive-target ones
  • Changed --add-dir and /add-dir in local terminal sessions to show the trust prompt for a folder you have not trusted yet; claude --bg refuses such a folder
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false to ignore more repository settings; set such values in user or managed settings
  • Changed how permission answers over Remote Control and on self-hosted runners save "always allow" choices
  • Changed enabled plugins that were refused for a malformed plugin.json display field: they now load, with their hooks and MCP servers; administrators should check the plugins they deploy
  • Changed how allowedHttpHookUrls and httpHookAllowedEnvVars apply to hooks from managed settings
  • Changed HTTP hooks to ignore Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding in their headers setting; the request's length comes from its body
  • Changed plugin uninstall to also delete the files extracted from the plugin's MCP bundles (.mcpb, .dxt), unless another plugin uses the same bundle
  • Changed some worktree sessions to skip some plugin settings; a notice names what was skipped
  • Changed /plugin uninstall, remove and switch questions to lists answered with the arrow keys and Enter, or Esc to cancel; y, n and u no longer answer them
  • Changed automatic compaction in plan mode to use the model answering you, such as Opus with opusplan, so it can cost more
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions to hold an organization's OpenTelemetry export until the first turn; a session that gets no message now sends nothing, so claude_code.session.count can fall
  • Changed Claude's messages to a session on another machine to be refused when your session uses an API key, auth token, profile or workload identity beside a saved claude.ai login
  • Changed --bare sessions on an unapproved API key: moving one to the background is now refused in most setups, and claude --bare --bg exits with an error if the background service lacks the key
  • Changed "Continue automatically at usage limit" to stop with a notice, sending nothing, when your login changes or ends during the wait
  • Remote Control: Changed how it connects through a proxy: requests now use a CONNECT tunnel, so a proxy that refuses CONNECT stops Remote Control with an error
  • Remote Control: Changed the session debug logs written under --verbose to go to ~/.claude/child-logs/
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Linux and macOS sessions with no gh to get a built-in gh api by default, via Anthropic, which adds their GitHub sign-in, if any; --use-anthropic-gh false turns it off
  • Changed agent view so that quitting with Ctrl+C twice, Ctrl+D twice or /exit after pressing ← in an empty conversation ends that session, instead of leaving it running for 5 minutes
  • Changed --await-initialize to be refused with --bg or --worktree --tmux, which never read the initialize request, instead of starting without the fields it carries
  • Changed worktree creation, /teleport and IDE checkouts to run git with a stricter PATH; a git filter or helper may need its full path
  • Changed the card for approving a subagent's plan to two choices, "Yes, and switch to default (ask each time) for this session" and "No", chosen with the arrow keys and Enter (typed text moves to No)
  • Changed the /claude-api skill to build agents on Managed Agents by default, unless you want to host the agent loop yourself
  • Changed /usage in fullscreen mode to show plan limit bars before session cost for subscribers; /cost still starts with cost
  • Changed the wording of some messages that claude subcommands print; JSON output is unchanged
  • Changed first-run setup to preselect the "Auto (match terminal)" theme instead of Dark mode
  • Changed fullscreen /cd to refuse "Yes" while its trust prompt doesn't fit, with a line saying to make the window taller
  • Removed the tmux notice that said the mouse wheel needs set -g mouse on in fullscreen; the wheel scrolls without it
  • Removed the spinner tip that suggested /clear 30 minutes into a running turn
  • [VSCode] Added a claudeCode.promptSuggestions setting that turns prompt suggestions off
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Rewind code to here" in a forked conversation sometimes undoing one turn too many and deleting files created in that turn
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Sandbox dialog creating empty files and folders in the home directory and the project's .git folder while the sandbox is off
  • [VSCode] Fixed the saved sign-in being lost on some networks
  • [VSCode] Fixed sign-in ending when a verification code, a web address or a code from another sign-in attempt is pasted; the panel now says what to paste instead
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen showing briefly each time a panel or window opened while signed in to Console without an API key
  • [VSCode] Fixed the usage-limit banner's "Request more" button for Team and Enterprise members coming back after each press without sending anything, after you signed in again during a session
  • [VSCode] Fixed /ide in a second Claude Code session silently losing the editor connection back to the first session; the newest connection now wins and the displaced session shows how to switch back
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved memories not being listed in the Memory dialog, or RAM use growing without end, when the memory folder held symlink loops, and a hang when it held a named pipe
  • [VSCode] Fixed a running command's live output stopping after one failed read
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Open in Terminal" showing only the shell's error when claude could not be started: in bash, zsh, fish and Git Bash, a notice now explains why and links to the install guide
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing no "Open artifact" link after Claude publishes an artifact
  • [VSCode] Fixed the prompt suggestion hiding the "attach selected text" hint while the chat panel is unfocused
  • [VSCode] Fixed buttons with no visible border in the high-contrast themes, and the dark welcome art on the sign-in screen in Light High Contrast
  • [VSCode] Improved Edit and Write speed: no wait for new problems on files that are not open in a tab when the editor has been reporting none for such files
  • [VSCode] Changed a running command's live output in the chat to look like the command card's OUT row
  • [VSCode] Changed the text of extension errors in event listeners, views and activation to stay out of the editor's own error telemetry

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
